_changelog: v1.0.1 (2026-10-10) Season 2 review fixes: RabbitMQ 4.3's delivery limit counts only failed deliveries, so a nack requeue never reaches it (u/returned_mail_dorota, explain step 4, the quorum queue real-world note, the Delivery limit term, the source title), with a new basic.nack and basic.reject term; the oldest-ticket commenter is renamed u/oldest_ticket_augustin, since s2e12 already has a character with the old name; the cold case no longer gives a dead-letter count the two workers couldn't reach; the Builders' Library note quotes the article, not Amazon, and gives its real reason for watching age; the redrive source carries its current page title; the guide comment drops the producer and consumer definitions; RabbitMQ is introduced as a message broker; recall r4's options balanced and its answer moved to index 3; option D trimmed; recall and cold case fragments tightened
title: The Queue Outside

post.author: u/brindle_lane_door
post.title: I work the door at a club. Since June, one ticket has come back to the top of the box every 1.5 seconds. Last night a second one joined it.

blocks.text: I work the door at the Mothlight, a club in two railway arches on Brindle Lane. We open at 22:00, and a guest arrives about every 10 seconds. They scan a code by the door, type a name and an email address, and the club's web server signs them up. Nobody gets in until their phone says *You're on the list*. The welcome email carries the code that gets them back in after a smoke. Fenna, who built the app, says saving a signup takes 0.1 seconds, the email provider takes 1.5 seconds to send one, and the server works on 8 signups at once.

Until May, the server sent the email before it answered. Every Saturday at 23:00 the late train empties onto Brindle Lane, and about 600 people sign up in a minute, 10 a second. The server could finish 5 a second. Phones spun for up to a minute and the line froze on the pavement. It was like walking every guest to the cloakroom myself.

In May Fenna changed it. Now the server saves the signup, drops a ticket in what she calls the box, and answers at once with the ticket number, which is also the guest's hook in Clodagh's cloakroom. Two workers take tickets off the top of the box and send the emails. If a send fails, the ticket goes back on top and is tried again. The line hasn't stopped since.

On Saturday 13 June, guest 413 typed *back for my coat* where his email address should go. He never came back. Worker-1 has tried his email every 1.5 seconds since that night, about 6.9 million times, Fenna says, and every Saturday since, the late train's emails have come up to 14 minutes late. His green wool coat is still on hook 413. Clodagh has taken it to lost property three times. Every Saturday it's back on the hook.
Last night at 02:00, ticket 2035 signed up with a comma where the dot goes. Fenna's log:

02:00:00.1  #2035  saved. answered 202. worker-2 takes it
02:00:01.6  worker-2  #2035 failed: not an email address. back on top
02:00:03.1  worker-2  #2035 failed: not an email address. back on top
02:30:00.0  box: 179 waiting, oldest 1,790 s
03:00:00.0  door shut. box: 359 waiting, oldest 3,590 s
05:00:00.0  box: 359 waiting, oldest 10,790 s
Nothing has left the box since 02:00. At 02:30 a man came back to the door with his phone held up. It still said *Welcome email: on its way*.
What should Fenna change before next Saturday?

blocks.label: fenna_dashboard_sat_0300.png

diagram.aria: Fenna's dashboard at 03:00:00 on Saturday. The door has shut. The web server still answers each signup with 202 in 0.1 seconds and has handed out 2,394 tickets tonight. The box, a queue, holds 359 tickets, the oldest waiting 3,590 seconds. Both workers are stuck: they send tickets 413 and 2035 to the email provider, which rejects them, and put them back on top. Nothing has been sent since 02:00.

blocks.caption: Fenna's dashboard at 03:00:00, redrawn. The web server still answers every signup with a 202 in 0.1 seconds, so the door never stopped. But both workers are retrying tickets that can't be sent: worker-1 has been on 413 since June, and worker-2 has been on 2035 since 02:00:00.1. Each failed ticket goes back on top and the same worker takes it again at once. Nothing has been sent since 02:00, and the box holds 359 tickets, the oldest waiting 3,590 seconds.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Some words first, then questions. Work done while the guest waits for the answer is synchronous: before May, the email was sent inside the request. Work done after the answer is asynchronous, or background work. The web server puts the emails on a queue, Fenna's box, as jobs, and the workers take them off and do them. And 202 Accepted is the status code for what the server says now: I have your request, and it isn't finished. Now the evidence. Before May, 8 signups at once at 1.6 seconds each: how many a second, against the 10 the late train brings? Since June, how many workers have really been sending? Since 02:00, how many? Why did the door keep moving all night while nothing left the box? And what in Fenna's code ever decides that a ticket won't be tried again?

replies.author: u/brindle_lane_door
replies.text: Fenna did the sums: 5 a second against 10, so before May the line grew by 5 a second for the whole minute. Since June it's been one worker, about 0.7 a second, and since 02:00, none. On festival nights we get a guest a second all night, and she's glad last night wasn't one. Your last question she answered straight away. Nothing does.

comments.author: u/returned_mail_dorota
comments.text: Post offices had a name for letters they could neither deliver nor send back: dead letters, opened in a dead letter office to find out where they belonged. This board should find that familiar. Queues borrowed it. A dead-letter queue, or DLQ, is a second queue where a message goes after failing a set number of times, instead of back on top. In Amazon SQS the number is maxReceiveCount, set in the queue's redrive policy. RabbitMQ's quorum queues have a delivery limit, 20 by default since version 4.0, though since 4.3 a message handed back with nack doesn't count. Two catches. A DLQ is a place to look, not a fix: alarm on it and make sure someone reads it. And don't set the limit so low that a provider's bad minute fills it with tickets that would have gone through on the next try.

comments.author: u/backoff_briony
comments.text: Fenna's loop has a name in RabbitMQ's docs. A message a consumer puts back is requeued to its original position if it can be, so at or near the head, and if the consumers keep putting it back, they make a requeue/redelivery loop. A message that can never succeed, like an address that isn't one, is a poison message. Retrying is right for failures that pass, like a 503 from a provider having a bad night, and then you wait a little longer between tries, with jitter. It's wrong for failures that can't. And mind the other direction: SQS delivers at least once. If a worker sends the email and dies before it deletes the ticket, the ticket comes back and someone sends it again. So make the job idempotent: before sending, check whether this ticket's email already went.

replies.author: u/brindle_lane_door
replies.text: Fenna says the provider had a bad night in August: one email in five failed the first time with a 503 and went through on the second. She hadn't thought about a guest getting the same email twice. Clodagh says that would be the least strange thing about this place.

comments.author: u/oldest_ticket_augustin
comments.text: Watch the age, not just the count. 359 tickets in a box could be a busy night; a ticket that has waited an hour is an outage. SQS reports both to CloudWatch: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible for how many are waiting, ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage for how long the oldest has waited. One odd detail: SQS leaves poison-pill messages, ones received again and again and never deleted, out of that age metric, so it wouldn't have shown you 413 itself, only the tickets piling up behind it. By my sums, an alarm at 10 minutes on the oldest ticket's age would have rung at about 23:11 every Saturday since June.

reply.prompt: Next Saturday the late train comes in at 23:00 as always. What should Fenna change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Go back to sending the email before answering, as before May, so a guest with a bad address finds out at the door.
options.part2: Fenna switched it back on Wednesday. On Saturday the late train came in at 23:00, and by 23:00:00.7 all 8 threads were busy. The server finished 5 signups a second against 10 arriving. At 23:01 there were 296 guests on the pavement waiting for a thread, and the p95 response time was 30.4 seconds. The slowest phone spun for 61.6 seconds, and the line didn't clear until 23:02:00.6. At 02:00 a guest typed a comma where the dot goes, and 3.1 seconds later his phone told him the email had failed. He fixed it at the door. That part worked. When we closed, the green wool coat was still on hook 413.
options.senior: Sending the email inside the request ties every signup to the slowest step: 8 threads at 1.6 seconds is 5 a second, and the late train brings 10. The one thing it did better, telling a guest about a bad address while he's still at the door, doesn't need it: check the address at signup, before the 202. The 2 AM problem was the retry rule, not the queue.

options.text: Run six workers instead of two, so even with a stuck ticket or two, the box empties within minutes of the rush.
options.part2: Fenna ran six workers on Saturday. Worker-1 was still on 413, but the other five took the late train's tickets: 399 in the box at 23:01, the last email sent at 23:03:00.5, two minutes after its guest signed up, and the box empty at 23:03:03.3. At 02:00 ticket 2035 came in with its comma, and a second worker started looping on it. By 03:00 the box was empty, and the two stuck workers had failed 12,005 times between them since just before 23:00. Fenna was pleased. I wasn't: two of six workers gone, and nothing to say so but a counter nobody watches. At 02:30 the man from ticket 2035 was at the door asking for his email, and when we closed his jacket was still on hook 2035, next to the green coat.
options.senior: More workers raise the drain rate, and that clears the rush sooner. But retrying forever means every poison ticket takes a worker for good: one since June, a second at 02:00, and the next bad address takes a third. Capacity doesn't fix a loop. Cap the tries, park the failures where someone will look, and then size the workers for the rush.

options.text: Give each ticket 3 tries, then throw it away, so a bad address can never hold a worker for more than 4.5 seconds.
options.part2: Fenna made the change on Wednesday. On Saturday at 22:59:51.5 ticket 413 failed its 6,854,401st try and was thrown away, and both workers went to the late train's tickets. The last one was sent at 23:07:30.2, and the box was empty at 23:08:01.6. At 02:00:04.6 ticket 2035 failed its third try and was thrown away too. Nothing on Fenna's dashboard changed colour. At 02:30 he was at the door with his phone, which still said *Welcome email: on its way*. Fenna searched for his ticket and couldn't find it anywhere: the box was empty, and there was nowhere else a ticket could be. When we closed there was a second coat nobody came back for, on hook 2035.
options.senior: Capping the tries frees the workers, and that's the right half. Throwing the ticket away is the wrong half: the guest never gets the email, and nobody can tell it happened or why. A dead-letter queue keeps the failed ticket where a person can read it, fix the cause and send it again, and an alarm on it says when to look.

options.text: Give each ticket 3 tries, then park it in a dead-letter queue; alarm on that queue and the oldest ticket's age.
options.part2: Fenna made the change on Wednesday, with one alarm for when the dead-letter queue holds anything and another for when the oldest ticket has waited 10 minutes. On Saturday at 22:59:51.5 ticket 413 failed its 6,854,401st try and went to the dead-letter queue, and her phone buzzed. Both workers took the late train: 519 tickets waiting at 23:01, the last email sent at 23:07:30.2 and the box empty at 23:08:01.6. The oldest ticket's age never passed 390 seconds, so the age alarm stayed quiet. At 02:00:04.6 ticket 2035 failed its third try and was parked, and her phone buzzed again. She read the address, put the dot back and sent it again by hand, and he had it before he left. Then she opened 413. Address: *back for my coat*. She marked it done. At closing, hook 413 was empty for the first time since June. Clodagh didn't see anyone take the coat.
options.senior: Retry what can pass and stop retrying what can't. A cap of 3 tries frees the worker, the dead-letter queue keeps the ticket so a person can fix it and send it again, and the two alarms cover the two ways a queue fails quietly: tickets that can't be sent, and tickets that wait too long. Next, wait between tries with backoff and jitter so a provider's bad night gets room to recover, check the address at signup before the 202, and make sending idempotent, because a ticket can be delivered twice.

sim.title: Run the box at the Mothlight
sim.lede: You're Fenna, replaying Saturday night at the Mothlight from 22:59:50. From 22:00 a guest signs up every 10 seconds; at 23:00 the late train brings 600 in a minute, 10 a second; the door shuts at 03:00. The web server works on 8 signups at once. Saving one takes 0.1 s, and the email provider takes 1.5 s per email. Before May the server sent the email before it answered, 1.6 s a signup; if the send failed it tried once more, and if that failed too it answered with an error. Since May it saves the signup, drops a ticket in the box and answers 202 at once, and free workers take the ticket on top and send the email. A failed ticket goes back on top, and the worker that failed it is the first one free, so it takes it again at once: the sim never waits between tries, so there's no backoff. Worker-1 starts on June's ticket 413, which has failed 6,854,400 times, once every 1.5 s for 119 days. At 02:00:00 ticket 2035 signs up with a comma where the dot goes. On the provider's bad night, every fifth email fails its first try with a 503 and goes through on the second. p95 and busy cover the last 10 seconds. A ticket's age counts from its guest's signup, and only while it waits in the box. Stuck counts tickets that have failed 3 or more times and are still being tried. Changing a setting replays the night. The clock runs 10 times faster than real life. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press nothing and watch the late train at 23:00: every guest is answered in 0.1 s, while the box climbs to 559 by 23:01 with only worker-2 sending. The oldest ticket passes 10 minutes at 23:10:42.9, the last guest off the train gets the email at 23:15:00.1, and the box is empty at 23:17:27.1. Switch to Before May: all 8 threads busy at 23:00:00.7, a p95 of 30.4 s at 23:01 and 61.6 s at 23:02:10. Back to Since May, pick 3 tries, then the dead-letter queue: 413 is parked at 22:59:51.5 and the box is empty at 23:08:01.6. Skip to 01:59:50 with each retry rule and watch ticket 2035, then skip to 03:00. Last, try a festival night with one worker, then two, and the provider's bad night.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the arches was haunted but the retry rule. Fenna's box let the web server answer every guest in 0.1 seconds, but a failed ticket went back on top forever, so ticket 413 has held a worker since June, and from 02:00 ticket 2035 held the other. With no dead-letter queue and no alarm on the oldest ticket's age, nobody saw the box stop.

steps.title: Slow work inside a request holds the guest and a thread.
steps.text: Before May every signup was synchronous: save for 0.1 seconds, send the welcome email for 1.5, then answer. The email was the bottleneck, and a thread was busy for the whole 1.6 seconds, so 8 threads finished at most 5 signups a second. The late train brings 10 a second for a minute, so the line grows by 5 a second: by 23:01, 296 guests are waiting for a thread, the p95 response time is 30.4 seconds, and the slowest guest watches a spinner for 61.6. Nothing about the email changes the answer the guest needs, which is "you're on the list". Work like that, sending an email, resizing an image, making a PDF, calling a slow dependency, is the first thing to move out of the request.

steps.title: Answer now, do it later: producers, a queue and workers.
steps.text: Since May the request does only what the guest needs: save the signup in the database, put a job on a queue, and answer 202 Accepted with the ticket number. That takes 0.1 seconds, so the whole rush keeps about one thread busy and the line never forms. The web server is the producer. The workers are consumers: each takes the job at the head of the queue, sends the email and takes the next, in parallel with the others. RFC 9110 calls 202 intentionally noncommittal: the work might still not happen, so the answer ought to point to a status monitor, here the phone screen that says the email is on its way. Keep the queue durable, so a restart loses no tickets. The cost: the email now arrives later than the answer, and if it never arrives, nobody is at the door to notice.

steps.title: A queue smooths a spike only if the workers drain it.
steps.text: A queue absorbs a burst: 600 tickets arrive in a minute and the workers send them at their own pace. While arrivals beat the drain rate, the backlog grows by the difference; afterwards it shrinks by the difference. Two workers at 1.5 seconds each drain about 1.3 a second, so the rush's last email goes out at 23:07:30.2, 390 seconds after its guest signed up. With worker-1 stuck on 413 it was one worker at about 0.7 a second, and 840 seconds. If arrivals stay above the drain rate, the backlog never drains: on a festival night, a guest a second, one worker sending about 0.7 a second leaves 5,344 tickets waiting at 03:00. Amazon's Builders' Library calls this bimodal: fine while you keep up, and a long recovery once you fall behind. More workers raise the drain rate; so does making each job cheaper.

steps.title: Retry what can pass, park what can't.
steps.text: A send can hit a transient failure that passes, like a 503 from a provider having a bad night, or a permanent failure that never will, like an address that isn't one. Fenna's rule put every failure back on top, and RabbitMQ's docs describe what follows: a requeued message goes back at or near the head, and consumers that keep requeueing it make a requeue/redelivery loop. A poison message in that loop holds a worker forever: 413 has failed about 6.9 million times. So cap the tries; for transient failures, wait between them with exponential backoff and jitter; and after the cap, move the job to a dead-letter queue, where it waits for a person instead of a worker. SQS does it with maxReceiveCount, and RabbitMQ's quorum queues with a delivery limit (since 4.3, failed deliveries only). A DLQ only helps if someone looks: alarm on it, fix the cause, then redrive the jobs. And because queues like SQS deliver at least once, a job can run twice, so make it idempotent, for example by using the ticket number as an idempotency key: record each send, and check for it before sending. Season 4 goes deeper.

steps.title: Watch the oldest job's age, not just the count.
steps.text: A queue hides trouble: the door looked fine all night while the box filled. Queue depth says how many jobs are waiting; the age of the oldest says how late the work is, which is what guests feel. 359 waiting at 03:00 could be a busy night, but an oldest ticket of 3,590 seconds is an outage. An alarm at 10 minutes on the oldest ticket's age would have rung at 23:10:42.9, when ticket 790 had waited 10 minutes, and SQS sends both numbers to CloudWatch. Order isn't promised either: a standard SQS queue only tries to keep it and may deliver messages out of order, and any retry reorders jobs. If order matters, use a FIFO queue, or make jobs that don't care.

diagram.aria: The fix, replayed for Saturday from 22:59:50 to 03:00. Guests' phones send 10 signups a second at 23:00. The web server answers each with 202 and the ticket number in 0.1 seconds and drops a ticket in the box, which holds 519 at 23:01 and is empty by 23:08:01.6. Both workers send, 3 tries per ticket. Tickets that fail 3 tries go to the dead-letter queue, which holds 2, tickets 413 and 2035, with an alarm at the first. The alarm on the oldest ticket's age, at 10 minutes, stays quiet: the oldest never passes 390 seconds.

explain.caption: The fix, replayed for Saturday with 3 tries and a dead-letter queue. The web server still answers every signup with a 202 in 0.1 seconds. Ticket 413 is parked at 22:59:51.5 on its 6,854,401st failed try, and the dead-letter queue's alarm rings. Both workers take the late train's tickets: 519 waiting at 23:01, the last email sent at 23:07:30.2 and the box empty at 23:08:01.6. The oldest ticket's age never passes 390 seconds, so the age alarm stays quiet. Ticket 2035 is parked at 02:00:04.6 after 3 tries, and the alarm rings again.

fix.title: The fix: cap the tries, park failures in a dead-letter queue, and alarm on it and on the oldest ticket's age
fix.text: Give each ticket 3 tries. Between tries, wait with exponential backoff and jitter, so a provider's bad night gets room to recover; the sim retries at once and leaves that out. After the third failure, move the ticket to a dead-letter queue instead of back on top, so the worker moves on. Alarm when the dead-letter queue holds anything, and when the oldest ticket in the box has waited 10 minutes. Then read what's parked, fix the cause and redrive it. Add validation at signup, before the 202, so a guest with a comma in the address hears about it at the door. Make sending idempotent: record each ticket's send and check before sending, because a ticket can be delivered twice. And size the workers for the rush: with two sending, the late train's last email goes out at 23:07:30.2.

limits: The guest waits longer for the result. The answer is fast, but the email arrives seconds or minutes later, and if it fails the guest has already gone in. Anything the guest needs before the answer, like a check that the address looks real, has to stay in the request, and the rest needs a status monitor the guest can check.

A queue moves trouble out of sight. Without alarms on the oldest job's age and on the dead-letter queue, a stuck worker or a slow drain shows up only when someone complains. And a backlog has to be paid back: while work arrives faster than the drain rate, it waits, however big the queue.

Order and single delivery aren't promised. A standard SQS queue delivers at least once and only tries to keep order, and every retry reorders jobs, so jobs should be idempotent and shouldn't depend on order unless you use a FIFO queue.

explain.seniorTake: Keep in the request only what the user needs before the answer, and put the rest on a queue: answer 202 with a way to check, and let workers do it at their own pace. Then design for failure from the first day. Jobs will fail, some for a moment and some forever, so cap the tries, back off between them, park what still fails in a dead-letter queue, and make jobs idempotent, because they will sometimes run twice. Size the workers so the drain rate beats the arrival rate after a spike, and watch the oldest job's age as well as the depth, with alarms on it and on the dead-letter queue. A queue nobody watches is a place where work disappears quietly.

realWorld.title: 202 Accepted, in RFC 9110
realWorld.text: RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics (June 2022), defines 202 Accepted as a request that has been accepted for processing, but whose processing has not been completed, and says it might or might not eventually be acted upon. There is no facility in HTTP for re-sending a status code from an asynchronous operation. The RFC calls the response intentionally noncommittal: it lets a server accept a request for some other process, perhaps a batch-oriented one run once per day, without the client's connection staying open until it's done, and the response ought to describe the request's current status and point to (or embed) a status monitor that can estimate when it will be fulfilled.

realWorld.title: SQS hides a message; it doesn't remove it
realWorld.text: Amazon SQS doesn't remove a message when a consumer receives it. It hides it for the visibility timeout, 30 seconds by default and at most 12 hours, and the consumer deletes it when it's done. If it isn't deleted before the timeout expires, the message becomes visible again and can be retrieved by another consumer. Because of the at-least-once delivery model, the docs add, there's no absolute guarantee that a message won't be delivered more than once during the visibility timeout. Among the best practices on the same page: configure a dead-letter queue, so messages that keep failing stop circulating in the main queue.

realWorld.title: SQS dead-letter queues
realWorld.text: SQS lets a source queue target a dead-letter queue for messages that aren't processed successfully, and the docs say DLQs are useful for debugging because you can isolate unconsumed messages to find out why processing failed. maxReceiveCount is how many times a consumer can receive a message before it moves to the DLQ: set it as low as 1 and one failure moves it, so the docs advise setting it high enough to allow for sufficient retries. They also note that in a standard queue whose maxReceiveCount is greater than 3, a message received 3 or more times without being deleted is moved to the back of the queue, and that a DLQ's retention period should be longer than its source queue's.

realWorld.title: At least once, so make it idempotent
realWorld.text: The SQS docs explain why a message can come back after you delete it: SQS stores copies on several servers, and if one of them is unavailable when you delete the message, its copy can be delivered again later. Their advice is to design applications to be idempotent, so they aren't affected adversely when they process the same message more than once.

realWorld.title: Standard queues: best-effort order
realWorld.text: SQS standard queues ensure at-least-once delivery, but because of their highly distributed architecture, more than one copy of a message might be delivered and messages may occasionally arrive out of order, though they make a best-effort attempt to keep the order they were sent in. The page lists decoupling live user requests from intensive background work as a use case.

realWorld.title: What SQS lets you watch
realWorld.text: SQS sends CloudWatch metrics for every queue. ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible reflects the current processing backlog, and the docs say a consistently high value may point to too few consumers or stuck processing logic; for a dead-letter queue it's the metric to alarm on. ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage is the age of the oldest unprocessed message. One caveat: poison-pill messages, those received again and again but never deleted, are left out of that age metric until they're processed successfully, so it shows the work piling up behind a stuck message rather than the stuck message itself.

realWorld.title: A dead-letter queue still forgets
realWorld.text: SQS keeps a message for 4 days by default, and the retention period can be set from 60 seconds up to 1,209,600 seconds, 14 days. So a dead-letter queue nobody reads still loses what it holds when the retention period runs out, which is one more reason to alarm on it.

realWorld.title: Redrive, after the fix
realWorld.text: Once the cause is fixed, SQS's dead-letter queue redrive moves unconsumed messages from a DLQ to another destination for processing, by default back to the source queue, at a speed you can cap with a custom maximum of up to 500 messages a second.

realWorld.title: RabbitMQ: the requeue loop
realWorld.text: RabbitMQ, a message broker, documents consumer acknowledgements, and its docs say a requeued message is placed at its original position in its queue if possible, or otherwise closer to the head, and may be immediately ready for redelivery. If all consumers requeue because they can't process a delivery for a transient reason, they create a requeue/redelivery loop, costly in network bandwidth and CPU. Consumers can track the number of redeliveries and reject messages for good, or requeue after a delay. Any delivery not acknowledged when its connection closes is requeued automatically, so consumers must be prepared for redeliveries and built with idempotence in mind.

realWorld.title: RabbitMQ: poison messages and the delivery limit
realWorld.text: RabbitMQ's quorum queues handle poison messages, which its docs describe as messages that make a consumer requeue a delivery over and over, so it's never consumed completely and positively acknowledged. Since RabbitMQ 4.0 their delivery limit defaults to 20: a message redelivered more times than that is dropped, or moved to a dead-letter queue if one is configured. The docs recommend a dead letter configuration on every quorum queue so messages aren't dropped and lost by accident, and advise against disabling the limit, because repeated requeues can threaten the stability of the queue and the RabbitMQ servers. Since RabbitMQ 4.3 the limit counts only failed deliveries, such as a consumer crash or a basic.reject, so a consumer that hands a message back with basic.nack can requeue it forever without reaching the limit: count the tries in the consumer too.

realWorld.title: Amazon: alarm on the age
realWorld.text: The Amazon Builders' Library article Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs says a queue increases a system's durability and availability at the price of occasional increased latency due to retries, and that when processing stops but messages keep arriving, a large backlog can make work complete too late to be useful. It warns that even short load spikes can mean multi-hour recovery times. The team alarms if there are any messages in a dead-letter queue, because that means a bug to fix, and the DLQ lets it re-process the messages after the fix. But DLQ information arrives too late to rely on alone, and the latency producers see only mirrors the queue service's own, so it focuses more on measuring the age of messages in the queue, which quickly catches systems that are behind or erroring out and retrying.

asked: When would you use a queue instead of doing the work in the request?
What happens if the consumer is slower than the producer?
What is a dead-letter queue for?
interview.answer: Use a queue when the work doesn't change the answer the user needs right now and is slow, or depends on something slow or unreliable: sending email, resizing images, making PDFs, calling a third party. The request saves what it must, puts a job on a durable queue and answers at once, often with 202 Accepted and a way to check the status; workers do the job at their own pace, and a spike waits in the queue instead of holding threads. If consumers are slower than producers, the backlog grows by the difference for as long as that lasts. A short spike is fine if the workers drain it afterwards; a steady shortfall grows without bound, and the age of the oldest message grows with it. Add consumers or make each job cheaper, and if you still can't keep up, slow the producers down or turn some work away; either way, alarm on the oldest message's age, not only the depth. A dead-letter queue is where a message goes after failing a set number of times, maxReceiveCount in SQS, so a poison message stops holding a worker and isn't lost: alarm on it, read it, fix the cause and redrive. Then mention the details: retry transient failures with backoff and jitter, cap the tries, and make jobs idempotent, because most queues deliver at least once.

terms.def: Done while the caller waits: the answer comes only after the work is finished. Before May, the Mothlight's server sent each welcome email inside the signup request.
Done after the answer, so the caller doesn't wait for it. Also called background work.
A queue of jobs that workers do after the request has been answered, so slow work doesn't hold the user or a thread.
One piece of work put on a queue to be done later, like sending one welcome email.
A program that puts jobs on a queue. At the Mothlight it's the web server.
A program that takes jobs off a queue and does them. Also called a worker.
A consumer: a program that takes the next job from a queue, does it, then takes the next. The Mothlight has two, sending welcome emails.
One item on a queue, such as a job. SQS and RabbitMQ call them messages.
A server that holds queues and hands messages from producers to consumers, such as RabbitMQ.
Fenna's word for a job in the box: one guest's welcome email, numbered. The number is also the guest's hook in the cloakroom.
Fenna's name for the Mothlight's queue of tickets. A free worker takes the ticket on top; in her version, a failed one goes back on top.
One guest's form, a name and an email address, sent to the club's web server to put them on the list.
The email a guest gets after signing up, with the code that lets them back in after a smoke.
A service that sends email for you. Your app hands it each message, and it answers whether the send was accepted.
The status code for a request accepted for processing but not finished. The answer should say where to check on it.
RFC 9110's name for something that shows a request's current status and an estimate of when it will be done. At the Mothlight, the phone screen saying the email is on its way.
Work waiting to be done, here the tickets in the box. It grows while jobs arrive faster than workers finish them, and shrinks when they arrive slower.
How many messages are waiting in a queue right now.
How long the message at the front of a queue has waited. It shows a stuck or slow queue even when the depth looks normal.
How fast workers take jobs off a queue: the number of workers divided by the time a job takes. Two workers at 1.5 s each drain about 1.3 a second.
The front: the next message to be handed out. Fenna calls it the top of the box.
To put a message that couldn't be handled back on the queue, so it can be delivered again.
Handing a message to a consumer again after it was requeued or never acknowledged.
RabbitMQ's name for consumers putting a message back and getting it again, over and over, which costs network and CPU and gets nothing done.
A message that fails every time it's tried, like an email address with a comma in it, so retrying can never work. Also called a poison pill.
A failure that may pass if you try again later, like a 503 from a busy provider.
A failure that will happen every time, like an address that isn't an email address. Retrying it wastes the worker.
A separate queue where messages go after failing a set number of times, so they stop holding up the main queue and a person can look, fix the cause and send them again.
A post office department that opened letters it could neither deliver nor return, to find out where they belonged.
The setting in an SQS redrive policy: how many times a message can be received before it's moved to the dead-letter queue.
The SQS settings on a queue that name its dead-letter queue and its maxReceiveCount.
Moving messages from a dead-letter queue back to a queue for processing, usually after fixing what made them fail.

In a RabbitMQ quorum queue, how many times a message may be redelivered before it's dropped or sent to a DLQ, 20 by default since 4.0. Since 4.3 only failed deliveries count, not messages a consumer hands back with nack.

Two ways a RabbitMQ consumer can refuse a message, putting it back on the queue if it asks to. Since 4.3 a reject counts toward a quorum queue's delivery limit and a nack, short for basic.nack, doesn't.
A RabbitMQ queue type that keeps copies on several servers and counts how many times each message has been delivered.
How long SQS hides a message after a consumer receives it. If it isn't deleted by then, it becomes visible again and another consumer can get it. 30 seconds by default.
Telling the queue a message is done so it's removed. In SQS a consumer deletes a message after handling it; until then it's only hidden.
A promise that every message is delivered, sometimes more than once. The consumer has to cope with copies.
SQS's default queue type: at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering, so messages can arrive out of order.
First in, first out: an SQS queue type that keeps messages in the order they were sent.
How long a queue keeps a message before deleting it. SQS keeps one 4 days by default, and up to 14.
Simple Queue Service: AWS's managed message queue.
A widely used message broker that teams often run on their own servers.
A file format for documents that look the same on every screen and printer, like a receipt or a ticket.
The SQS CloudWatch metric for the age of the oldest unprocessed message in a queue.
The SQS CloudWatch metric for how many messages are waiting to be received: the backlog.
A CloudWatch rule that watches one metric and notifies someone when it crosses a line you set, like a queue's oldest message passing 10 minutes.
Checking input when it arrives, such as whether an email address looks like one, so bad data is turned away while the user is still there to fix it.
A time when a system isn't doing its job for its users, even if parts of it still answer.
Finding out why a program went wrong.
Amazon's collection of articles by its engineers on how Amazon builds and runs services.
Having two modes. A queue-based system is quick while it keeps up and very slow once a backlog builds, with little in between.

atWork: Think of a signup flow that sends its welcome email inside the request: when the email provider slows down, signups time out. Find one like it in a system you can read, any request that waits on an email, a PDF, an image or a third-party call. Read-only access is enough. How long does that step take at p95, and how many threads does the server have? If the work is already on a queue, open the queue's settings: is there a redrive policy with a dead-letter queue, and what's maxReceiveCount? In CloudWatch, chart ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage and ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible for the queue and its DLQ over the last busy day. Is there an alarm on the oldest message's age, and one on any message in the DLQ? Do the workers back off between tries, and is sending idempotent? If not, draft the fix: answer 202 and put the job on a queue, workers with capped retries, backoff and jitter, a DLQ, and alarms on the queue's age and on the DLQ.

recall.prompt: Your shop's checkout makes a PDF receipt before it answers. A PDF takes 3 seconds, the server handles 20 checkouts at once, and on sale days checkouts time out. What would you change, and what new things do you have to watch afterwards?

keyIdeas.idea: Move the PDF out of the request: save the order, put a job on a queue, answer at once, and let workers make the PDF
Each checkout holds a thread for the whole 3 seconds, so 20 at once is under 7 checkouts a second
Jobs can fail and can run twice: capped retries with backoff, a dead-letter queue, and idempotent jobs
Watch the queue's depth and its oldest job's age, and give the customer a way to check on the receipt

recall.model: Making the PDF doesn't change whether the order went through, so it doesn't belong in the request. Each checkout holds a thread for 3 seconds, so 20 at once is under 7 checkouts a second, and on a sale day the rest wait until they time out. Save the order, put a make-the-receipt job on a queue and answer at once, with the order page or 202 and a link to check; workers make the PDF and email it. Then plan for failure: retry with backoff and a cap, send what keeps failing to a dead-letter queue with an alarm, and make the job idempotent, because it may run twice. Watch the queue's depth and the age of its oldest job, and size the workers so they drain a sale-day backlog.

recall.prompt: Signups arrive at 10 a second for one minute. Two workers each send one email every 1.5 seconds, and nothing else is waiting. About how many tickets are waiting when the minute ends?
recall.why: Two workers send about 1.3 a second, so in 60 seconds they send about 80 of the 600. The Mothlight's sim, with 413 parked, has 519 waiting at 23:01. The backlog grows by arrivals minus the drain rate, and shrinks afterwards by the drain rate minus arrivals.

recall.prompt: Orders arrive at 50 a second all day. Your three workers can process 40 a second between them. What happens to the queue over the day, and what do you do about it?

keyIdeas.idea: The backlog grows by 10 a second without end: 36,000 an hour, and each order waits longer than the last
Raise the drain rate: more workers, or cheaper jobs
Alarm on the age of the oldest message, not only the depth
If you still can't keep up, slow the producers or turn work away instead of letting the queue grow

recall.model: The queue gains 10 orders a second, 36,000 an hour, and never drains: every order waits longer than the one before, so the age of the oldest message climbs all day. A queue only smooths a spike if the drain rate beats arrivals afterwards. Add a fourth worker or more, or make each order cheaper to process, so the drain rate tops 50 a second with room to spare. Alarm on the oldest message's age as well as the depth. If you still can't keep up, slow the producers down or turn some work away, instead of letting the backlog grow without bound.

recall.prompt: What is a dead-letter queue for?
options: Messages that arrive out of order, held back until the gap is filled
Spare room for messages when the main queue is full, so none are lost
Messages older than the queue's retention period, kept a little longer
Messages that failed too many times, kept for a person to fix and resend
recall.why: After maxReceiveCount receives in SQS, or the delivery limit in RabbitMQ, a failing message moves to the DLQ so it stops holding a worker and isn't lost. Alarm on it, read it, fix the cause and redrive. A DLQ isn't a fix by itself: it's a place to look.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Fenna moved the box to Amazon SQS, with a dead-letter queue after 3 receives and alarms on it and on the oldest ticket's age. In February the email provider slowed down, and a send started taking about 40 seconds. SQS gives a worker 30 seconds with a ticket before the others can see it again. That Saturday guests got two and three copies of the same welcome email, and by 23:30 the dead-letter queue was filling with tickets whose emails had all gone out.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did guests get the same email two and three times, why did sent tickets end up in the dead-letter queue, and what should Fenna change?

keyIdeas.idea: The send took longer than the visibility timeout, so the ticket became visible again and another worker sent it too
Each of those receives counted toward maxReceiveCount, so tickets that had really been sent reached the limit and went to the DLQ
Raise the visibility timeout above the slowest send, or extend it while a send runs, and put a timeout on the provider call
Make sending idempotent: record each ticket's send and check before sending

coldCase.model: SQS doesn't remove a ticket when a worker takes it; it hides it for the visibility timeout, 30 seconds here, and the worker deletes it when it's done. With sends taking 40 seconds, every ticket became visible again in the middle of its send, and another worker took it and sent it again: two or three copies. Each of those receives counted toward maxReceiveCount, so tickets that had really been sent reached 3 and were moved to the dead-letter queue. Raise the visibility timeout above the slowest send you expect, or extend it while a send is still running, and put a timeout on the provider call so a send can't run forever. Make sending idempotent, recording each ticket's send and checking it first, so a redelivered ticket sends nothing. Then redrive the parked tickets: the check skips the ones already sent.

sources.title: RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics (R. Fielding, M. Nottingham, J. Reschke, Eds., Standards Track, June 2022), section 15.3.3, 202 Accepted: accepted for processing but not completed; might or might not eventually be acted upon; intentionally noncommittal; point to (or embed) a status monitor

Amazon SQS Developer Guide: Amazon SQS visibility timeout (a message not deleted before the timeout becomes visible again and can be retrieved by another consumer; default 30 seconds; at-least-once delivery during the timeout; configure a dead-letter queue)

Amazon SQS Developer Guide: Using dead-letter queues in Amazon SQS (DLQs for messages not processed successfully, useful for debugging; maxReceiveCount; standard queues move messages received 3 or more times to the back when maxReceiveCount is greater than 3; DLQ retention longer than the source queue's)
Amazon SQS Developer Guide: Amazon SQS at-least-once delivery (copies on multiple servers; a copy can be delivered again; design applications to be idempotent)
Amazon SQS Developer Guide: Amazon SQS standard queues (at-least-once delivery, occasional out-of-order arrival, best-effort ordering; decoupling live user requests from intensive background work)

Amazon SQS Developer Guide: Available CloudWatch metrics for Amazon SQS (ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage, poison-pill messages excluded until processed successfully; ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible, the current processing backlog, the metric to alarm on for DLQs)
Amazon SQS Developer Guide: Amazon SQS message quotas (message retention 4 days by default, 60 seconds to 1,209,600 seconds; visibility timeout 30 seconds by default, up to 12 hours)

Amazon SQS Developer Guide: Learn how to configure a dead-letter queue redrive in Amazon SQS (moves unconsumed messages from a DLQ to another destination, by default the source queue; custom maximum velocity up to 500 messages per second)

RabbitMQ documentation: Consumer Acknowledgements and Publisher Confirms (a requeued message goes to its original position or closer to the head; requeue/redelivery loops; unacknowledged deliveries requeued when the connection closes; implement consumers with idempotence in mind)

RabbitMQ documentation: Quorum Queues (poison message handling; delivery limit defaults to 20 since RabbitMQ 4.0; since 4.3, delivery-count rather than acquired-count; nack returns don't count; dropped or dead-lettered past the limit; a dead letter configuration recommended; disabling the limit not recommended)

Amazon Builders' Library: Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs (durability and availability at the price of occasional increased latency; bimodal behavior; short load spikes and multi-hour recovery; alarm on any message in a DLQ; measure the age of messages in the queue)
